issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

Clinical Vignette: Arjun

Arjun was fifty-three when he arrived at the clinic, his shoulders rounded forward as if permanently braced against an invisible weight. He had been a painter for thirty years—commercial work mostly, the kind that built steady reputation and paid the mortgage on a modest house in New Jersey where he lived with his wife, Priya, and their adult son. That life, the one he had constructed with careful discipline and small pleasures, had fractured seventeen months ago when he returned from a two-week trip to visit relatives in Beirut. He had gone in March, before the situation deteriorated, or so he had believed. He was there when the shelling started—sudden, incomprehensible. He was walking to the market near his cousin's apartment when the first explosion came. The sound was not like anything he had ever heard, a concussive force that seemed to come from inside his own chest. The smell came next: cordite, dust, something burning that he could not name. Around him, people screamed and ran. He ran too, but in those seconds before he found shelter in a doorway, he felt the ground shift beneath him, felt the absolute absence of control—no choice about where to go, no time to think, only the animal certainty that death was arriving. He made it home. He was not physically injured. But something in him had shattered in a way that no bandage could address.

In the months that followed, Arjun found that certain smells—the acrid tang of paint thinner, a neighbor's charcoal grill, even the particular mustiness of the basement where he kept his supplies—would trigger a sudden cascade of physical alarm. His body would tense without his permission, his breath would shallow, and within seconds he would be flooded with the sense that danger was imminent, that he was once again powerless to prevent catastrophe. The sound of a car backfiring or a door slamming had the same effect; his startle response had become exaggerated, almost hair-trigger, and he found himself jumping at noises that his wife barely registered. These moments of sensory intrusion seemed to unlock something deeper. When the smell or sound hit, the memory would follow—not as a coherent narrative but as a bodily experience. His muscles would contract as if he were still crouched in that doorway, his chest would tighten as if the explosion were happening again, and he would be gripped by an overwhelming sense of loss and grief that had no clear target, a mourning not for anyone who had died but for something in himself that had been annihilated. The memory felt almost unreal in its intensity, too extreme to be something that had actually happened to him, yet his body insisted on its truth with every involuntary contraction.

What frightened Arjun most was the conviction that had crystallized over these seventeen months: the world was fundamentally dangerous, and he was no longer the person who could navigate it with competence. He had always taken pride in his work, in the steadiness of his hands and his eye for detail. Now he was certain he could not do those things anymore. Nothing felt meaningful—not the painting jobs that still came in, not the dinners his wife prepared, not the phone calls from his son. This conviction seemed to feed everything else. Because he believed the world was dangerous, he became hypervigilant, constantly monitoring for threat, unable to settle into ordinary moments. Because he felt he was no longer capable, he began to ruminate obsessively over why the event had happened to him, turning the question over and over as if the answer might somehow restore what he had lost. He threw himself into busyness—taking on more jobs than he could comfortably manage, working late into the evening, filling every gap with tasks and movement—as a way to outrun both the rumination and the memory itself. He stopped reading the news or watching television, convinced that any report of conflict or violence would trigger the same cascade of dread and bodily reenactment. His wife noticed that he had become distant, that he would disappear into the garage for hours, and that when she tried to talk to him about his experience, he would either shut down or become irritable. The busyness had a cost: he was exhausted, his work quality was beginning to slip, and the isolation was widening the gap between them.

What brought Arjun to seek help now was not a sudden crisis but an accumulation of small failures. He had made a significant mistake on a job—rushed, inattentive—and lost a client who had worked with him for years. His wife had finally told him, with tears in her eyes, that she felt like she was living with a ghost. He sat in the clinic chair with his hands folded, his body still tense even in a quiet room, and said quietly: "I need to know if I can be myself again. I don't know who I am now."
